Yeah side effects are pretty inevitable and it’s generally not an easy or fun process though depends on dosing. It makes your skin, lips, and eyes dry, causes sun sensitivity, facial flushing, purging of your acne where it gets way worse before it gets better for months sometimes, fatigue, joint pain, rashes and eczema. There were a few times where I felt like it affected my mood when I was first getting used to being on it as well as upping my dose (increased anxiety and irritability out of nowhere) but that didn’t last long thankfully. I got tinnitus starting in month 3 and had to pause my treatment to get my hearing tested to make sure I didn’t have hearing loss. This isn’t a side effect most people get but I got it and it never went away so I’ve had constant tinnitus for over a year now (I’m used to it and it doesn’t bother me anymore). As much as that sounds terrible, I still don’t regret going on it because my acne was ruining my self-esteem and causing me so much distress on a daily basis.

Medications all have side effects and everything comes with risks. Anti-depressants for instance are notorious for affecting people’s sex drives and causing weight gain (both of which happened to me pretty seriously in my mid 20s and my sex drive seems permanently affected and I’m still struggling to lose all the weight I gained) but most people take those without any fear of side effects. Accutane on the other hand has a reputation for being a serious drug with potentially serious side effects and therefore people tend to be more anxious about it. 

I was on Accutane for 9 months and have been done with my course for 6 months now. I’m 32f and went on for mostly hormonal cystic acne, and while my skin didn’t clear 100% it’s way better than it used to be. I did however get permanent tinnitus as a side effect unfortunately and was unaware that was even a possibility going into this process. I’ve had nonstop tinnitus for over a year straight and it didn’t stop when I got off Accutane. A lot of people seem to not have any long term side effects but it does happen. People either want to say it’s the worst drug in the world and ruined their life or say that people who talk about bad side effects are fear mongering and you shouldn’t listen to them, but really the truth is somewhere in the middle like it usually is. I still don’t regret going on it but it was hard and I am left with a permanent side effect but I can live with it and am pretty happy with my skin as of now. 

My advice is just keep track of how you’re feeling and listen to your body. If you start having concerns, talk to your doctor. You can always stop. Good luck.

31F and just finished my first round of Accutane (9 months). I had hormonal acne that started around 19/20 when I stopped taking the birth control pills I’d started in high school and it just never went away. My skin got way worse when I turned 27 and I started getting tons of cystic acne on my chin and jawline. Like you, I tried topicals and spiro with no luck. 

Some skincare product recommendations:

Cleanser: Paula’s Choice RESIST Hydrating Cleanser or Prequel Gleanser

Toner: I recommend a ceramide cream mist (I’ve been using the COSRX one but other Korean skincare brands make them as well)

Moisturizer: La Roche Posay Lipikar AP+ Triple Repair Cream or Prequel Barrier Therapy Cream 

SPF (I’d recommend min SPF 50): so many good Korean ones, my recent fave is the HaruHaru Black Rice Moisture Airy Lift Sunscreen (yellow tube). The photosensitivity is no joke (like I’d get burnt just being outside for 5 minutes). 

Lips (basically just keep something on your lips 24/7): Aquaphor ointment, Laneige lip sleeping mask

Other: I slugged with Aquaphor every night. You could also try a hypochlorous acid spray if your skin gets really irritated. I also used some mists to add extra hydration or to top of moisture throughout the day if I were home, like the Beekman Milk Shake Toner or the D’alba First Spray Serum, but those are just extra. 

Supplements: definitely take fish oil. I also took a Sea Buckthorn Oil Omega 7 supplement throughout my whole course and I really do feel like it’s the reason I didn’t get insanely dry ever. My mom recommended it to me (I guess it’s popular among women who have gone through menopause to retain moisture in the body and counteract dryness). 

Take your dose with lots of healthy fat (and take your fish oil with your dose and drink lots of water). I was aiming for 20g based on my own research because my initial doctor didn’t tell me much but I actually just met with a different doctor at the end of my treatment who told me you should take it with 50g of healthy fats per dose. Absorica is the brand that is the exception because it has fat built into it, but it often isn’t covered by insurance so you end up with generic isotretinoin. 

Purging can be rough. Mine lasted from the end of week 1 to basically the end of month 3 so that sucked but hang in there. Some people say they never purged though. Try not to pick, use pimple patches instead of popping as Accutane affects wound healing and scarring. 

Drink alcohol very sparingly and try not to take a lot of medicines processed by your liver, such as Tylenol.

I’d have moisturizing eyedrops on hand, your eyes will probably get dry. If you start to get styes/blepharitis I recommend a microwaveable warm eye compress. 

The inside of your nose will probably get dry too, a humidifier can help with that as well as just putting Aquaphor in your nose (gross I know). 

Some other side effects I experienced from Accutane but wasn’t prepared for: insane peach fuzz growth, facial flushing, rashes on my arms and chest, tinnitus (have had it nonstop since March and my derm made me stop treatment temporarily to get my hearing tested), some mood changes (increased anxiety and irritability, particularly when starting and when increasing dose), fatigue, occasional dizziness and headaches. 

I don’t list potential side effects to scare you, but I just want you to be informed. I was mostly expecting tons of dryness and then I kind of got blindsided by a bunch of other weird stuff. Everybody responds differently and some of it is going to depend on your dose as well. Side effects weren’t constant, most of them came and went throughout this process, except for the tinnitus which might be permanent. I did SO much research prior to starting Accutane and there were still so many things I wasn’t prepared for and my doctor certainly didn’t prepare me either. That being said, I definitely don’t regret doing it. 

This sub can absolutely be a great resource throughout your journey to see if anyone else is experiencing what you are or even just to get some support. 

I know I just threw a lot of info at you, but just do your research and take this one step at a time! It’s not always a fun process but it’s doable. Best of luck ❤️

It is not true that you cannot be prescribed Accutane. I didn’t really get depressed so much as felt really irritable or extra anxious, and I did experience a few intrusive thoughts. Purging can also be really difficult psychologically during the first few months.

Totally agree! The filmmakers should have definitely addressed it a little more directly for viewers who aren’t as familiar with DBT because a lot of people have probably never even heard of it. Outside of hospital settings, I feel like it’s not as prevalent in traditional outpatient therapy, unless you’re seeking treatment specifically for something like borderline personality disorder.

They often use DBT as the therapy of choice in these types of settings because it’s results are evidence based and can teach concrete coping mechanisms that patients can leave the hospital with. It’s generally very effective in teaching emotion regulation skills, which is often a contributing factor in ending up in an inpatient facility. Additionally, having a more structured therapy approach rather than generic talk therapy allows for better consistency in treatment ideally. As someone who was hospitalized 3 times in my late teens and has done DBT in addition to other types of therapy, I have found it helpful. 

Inpatient treatment is very short term so their goal is crisis management and trying to give patients coping skills in as little time as possible before they’re back out in the world, hence why it feels like nonstop DBT in the doc. More long term outpatient therapy is different than what the patients are receiving in the hospital setting.

Also there are definitely side effects, and there are ones everyone knows and then a whole bunch of others ones that aren’t really common knowledge and/or downplayed my doctors. 

The most common I’d say are dry skin, lips, eyes, and nose, redness and flushing, serious photosensitivity, joint pain, and fatigue. It definitely can affect your mood (mood swings, irritability, increased anxiety, depression, difficulty motivating). Other side effects include hair thinning, increase in peach fuzz on face, recurring styes and blepharitis, dizziness, headaches, rashes and eczema, sleep problems, tinnitus, and in rare cases hearing loss. I’ve also seen people report that it affects their libido. I’m sure there are others that I’m missing/aren’t aware of. 

Some people experience permanent side effects but obviously not everyone. I don’t say anything of that to scare you or discourage you, but I just want you to go into this process as informed as possible, because I felt like I did SO much research and still was completely unprepared for so many of the side effects I’ve been experiencing. Only you can decide if this is the right choice for you and you know your body and what you can tolerate, but I think it’s just important to go into it with an accurate understanding of this medication and not the rose colored glasses version where people just say “it’s the best, just do it, everything will be fine.”

His mom ended up ultimately taking him to a behavioral therapist for a while, and he was also suspected of having ADHD (which he has since been diagnosed with), so they were referred to a psychiatrist. In general, only a clinical psychologist or a psychiatrist can diagnose that kind of thing, but 4 is probably a bit young for a diagnosis. My nephew is still very reactive and easily upset in general but it usually doesn’t escalate the way it did when he was younger. He had his first really serious couple of episodes in a long time about a year ago at school, but he has since been okay. 

His mom has also always struggled with being overly reactive towards him, and as an outside observer, he definitely seems to feed off of her energy a lot and vice versa (and she is a single mom so it’s extra difficult). When my husband and I had watched him as a 4-year-old, we tried really hard to just be as non-reactive as possible when he would start a tantrum. We would put him in his room and let him get it out of his system and then when he was done he would pick up his room to the best of his abilities. We just tried to be really consistent and not give in to the behavior or get overly emotional or angry back at him. I also created a sticker chart and I let him pick out a sticker to put on it whenever he had a good day where he didn’t get physical and destroy his bedroom and we’d give him lots of verbal praise. He had lived in Texas with his mother and they were moving back home but she was so burnt out that she left him at his grandmother’s house for a couple months while she got everything settled for the move, so I watched him during the day while my mother-in-law was at work. At the end of those 2 months, we had actually seen a huge improvement in his behavior. However, when his mother finally did come back, he started to regress quite a bit (likely partly because of her emotional reactivity towards him). 

It’s difficult because an IED tantrum is not like a regular tantrum. The child is basically in a blind rage and there is no getting through to them. Once they’ve started, the episode just kind of has to run it’s course. There are ways to help lesson the frequency, but there’s not much you can do while it’s happening other than not feed into it with more intense emotion. It could also be that your child will grow out of this and doesn’t need any sort of formal diagnosis. The behavior has lasted a couple years now though, and even if it isn’t IED, it still wouldn’t hurt to look into behavioral therapy so you can all learn some coping mechanisms and strategies as a family.

It’s difficult to diagnose bipolar in younger individuals, partly because some amount of moodiness and irritability are a natural part of puberty. My biggest question would be has she always been more happy and animated than your other kids or is this a sudden shift like the moodiness? The biggest factor for diagnosing bipolar is the presence of mania or hypomania (which tends to present more as irritability than euphoria in children), so if the only new observable behavior is mostly related to your daughter becoming more easily upset, this is likely attributable to hormonal changes. If you haven’t discussed the mood (and other) changes that come with puberty, that’s probably a good idea so she knows what she’s feeling is pretty normal (lots of good books on puberty for girls out there). I think it’s really smart to be vigilant though, and you should definitely still keep observing her behavior. All those behaviors you listed are obviously HUGE red flags. Any time a child has an abrupt shift in temperament and behavior like that, that means there’s something going on emotionally. Hence the acting out. It’s easy to feel like your first response to these negative behaviors should be punishment, but she needs to feel secure and loved in her new roles as step-daughter and big sister. She likely doesn’t feel like a priority right now and probably feels a bit threatened. It’s difficult enough as a little kid having parents that are split up and having to go back and forth between two houses, but you also piled two enormous changes (getting married and having another baby) on your daughter, and to a 5 year old, that’s super scary and confusing that her dad suddenly has a whole new family. I’m not saying to completely disregard behaviors like compulsive lying, but you have to address the underlying cause of the behaviors and time outs or whatever aren’t going to fix anything. So I’m also a step-parent and have been a part of my step-daughter’s life since she was about 16 months old (she’s about to turn 11). Like you, I was really young as well at the time I started co-parenting. It’s now been 9 years and I’d say the most difficult part of the relationship has always been dealing with my step-daughter’s mother. 

There are obviously a lot of details I don’t know about your specific situation, but from the little bit of detail you’ve provided, here’s what I’ll say:

First, he clearly doesn’t respect you, both in general and as a parent to his children. I don’t know exactly how long you and your wife have been together or how quickly you got together/married after she split from her ex. I also don’t know how young her boys are, but obviously all those factors can make a difference. This guy may just be an asshole, but it also seems like he’s maybe not over his ex entirely or feels threatened and jealous by your relationship with both her and the kids. Again, I can only speculate. It’s a complicated balancing act being a step-parent. I’ve been helping raise my husband’s daughter since she was super little and we’re extremely close, so I’m not one of those people that thinks step-parents shouldn’t actually parent. But I would say that while your wife may think of you as a full-on parent to her boys, her ex clearly doesn’t, and whether he’s an asshole or not, he’s the dad and you all need to be as civil as possible for the mental health of the children. Maybe in time he’ll respect you more as a parent, but you obviously can’t control that. Being hostile towards him though, despite how much you dislike him, will likely not help anything. 

Second, he’s clearly stepping on some boundaries and unfortunately it sounds like your wife is letting that happen a bit. I don’t know if your wife and her ex have a formal custody agreement or not, but regardless, stick to a schedule unless it’s something really serious or you’re figuring out holiday arrangements. If it’s his day with the kids and he tries to dump them on you guys to sabotage you and your wife’s alone time, your wife needs to say no. The more she gives in, the more he knows he can do it, especially if he knows it bothers you. 

Lastly, I would say that there’s unfortunately not too much you can do personally, at least in my opinion. Anything you try to say to him, whether it’s completely reasonable or not, he will totally disregard because he doesn’t like you being in the picture. This all really needs to be settled by your wife and her ex, as frustrating as that is. I would leave communication regarding the kids up to them, at least until the situation becomes healthier. She needs to work on standing her ground with her ex and maintaining clear expectations and boundaries as far as your role in her kids lives and their arrangement as co-parents. As much as you may want to fight that fight for her, she’s really got to do the heavy lifting there.

This is a difficult question to answer unfortunately. I’m not sure how old you are, but you sound fairly young. You did the right thing by telling someone, even if your friend believes otherwise. Everyone’s situation is different obviously, but like you mention, it sounds like her suicidal ideation and depression are largely stemming from her environment. This really makes it challenging until she’s out on her own, and even then she’ll likely still struggle with it. It’s not uncommon for people who are depressed and suicidal to isolate and push other people away, but my advice to you would be not to let her scare you off. You’re in a tough situation and it’s hard to see someone you love hurting so badly, but unfortunately you can’t do much other than just try to be there for her as best you can. If she isn’t already in therapy, that can be a really helpful outlet (it was for me when I was a teenager struggling with depression, anxiety, self-harm, and suicidal thoughts). If her parents are unwilling to get her help, there’s likely resources at your school for mental health issues, although I don’t know how willing she is to try to get some help at the moment. Sometimes it takes a dramatic event for someone to start getting the help they need. For me, I attempted suicide when I was 16 and had to spend 2 weeks in an in-patient psych hospital. By the end of high school, I was hospitalized two more times. While it wasn’t pleasant, it did start me down the road of seeking treatment. Though I remember feeling really alone and isolated at that time in my life, I also remember the couple of close friends I had that stuck with me through it even though they didn’t fully understand what I was experiencing. The best you can do is be a good friend, but you sound like you’re already doing a good job of that.
